prompt.context: Our client, Big Bob's RV Generator Co., makes high efficiency generators for RVs. Recently, profits have been declining. Bob has hired your team to figure out why and what can be done to improve profitability.
prompt.question: Why have profits been declining, and what can be done to improve profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Does Big Bob have other product lines?
clarifying_info.a: No. Big Bob only makes generators.

clarifying_info.q: Does Bob make more than one type of generator?
clarifying_info.a: No. Bob only makes one type of generator.
Bob sells generators to a large RV manufacturer who uses them as a component in their RV products. This is Bob's only customer.

clarifying_info.q: What kind of generator does Bob make?
clarifying_info.a: High efficiency generators — the highest quality but also highest price generator. Think of it as the BMW of RV generators.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other competitors in the high efficiency generator market?
clarifying_info.a: No. Bob is the only player in the high efficiency generator market.

framework: Diagnose profit decline: decompose into Revenue vs. Cost drivers
Revenue side: price changes, volume changes (customer demand, market size), new customer / market opportunities
Cost side: COGS (materials, labor, manufacturing), fixed costs (SG&A, overhead), supplier pricing
Competitive landscape: new entrants threatening Bob's monopoly position
Strategic response: defend existing market, expand into adjacent markets, develop lower-cost product line

questions.prompt: Question 1: What are some strategies for improving profitability?
questions.guidance: Push candidate to segment ideas into Revenue and Cost categories. Strong answers cover multiple levers in each bucket.

questions.prompt: Question 2: A new player, Company A, is threatening to enter the high efficiency generator market with a lower quality and lower priced generator. What should Bob do?
questions.guidance: Company A's new generator will be $250 cheaper than Bob's. Bob is able to create a lower quality generator himself sooner than the competitor. Candidate should consider matching the lower price point, launching a flanking lower-quality product, and should ask about cost information before deciding. Push candidate to justify any price they recommend for Bob's potential lower-quality generator.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Calculate the contribution margins of Bob's high-quality and low-quality generators. Then calculate the breakeven number of units the new generator must sell to equal current profits.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate contribution margin and per-unit contribution for each generator, then solve for breakeven units given fixed costs and current volume.

math.setup: Existing generator: Price $5,000, COGS $3,000. New generator: Price $4,750, COGS $2,950. Annual fixed costs: $10,000,000. Annual existing generator units sold: 10,000.
steps: Existing generator contribution margin: ($5,000 - $3,000) / $5,000 = 40%; contribution per unit = $2,000
New generator contribution margin: ($4,750 - $2,950) / $4,750 = 38%; contribution per unit = $1,800
Breakeven units for new generator (to match $10M profit): ($10,000,000 + $10,000,000) / $1,800 = 11,111 units
Bob would need to sell 1,111 more units of the new generator than current sales to maintain the same profitability
math.answer: Breakeven = 11,111 units of new generator; 1,111 additional units required vs. current 10,000

questions.prompt: Question 4: If Bob does NOT launch a new generator, current unit sales will drop 45% when the competitor enters. If Bob DOES launch the new generator, he will retain all sales but 45% of existing generator sales will be cannibalized by the new generator. What should Bob do?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate profit under both scenarios and compare. The scenario with the new generator yields significantly higher profit.

math.setup: Use existing: Price $5,000, COGS $3,000, $2,000 contribution. New: Price $4,750, COGS $2,950, $1,800 contribution. Fixed costs $10M. Base volume 10,000 units.
steps: Scenario B — Launch new generator: Old generator units = 10,000 × 0.55 = 5,500; Old contribution = 5,500 × $2,000 = $11,000,000; New generator units (cannibalized) = 10,000 × 0.45 = 4,500; New contribution = 4,500 × $1,800 = $8,100,000; Total profit = $11,000,000 + $8,100,000 - $10,000,000 = $9,100,000
math.answer: Scenario A profit = $1M; Scenario B profit = $9.1M. Bob should launch the new generator.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the strategies Big Bob could pursue to improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing
ideas: Increase price of existing high-efficiency generator
Introduce tiered pricing or premium configurations
Price new lower-quality generator to undercut Company A pre-emptively

categories.name: Revenue — Volume & Customers
ideas: Sell direct to consumers for non-RV uses (home backup, tailgating, construction)
Expand into adjacent OEM markets (marine, truck, industrial)

categories.name: Revenue — New Streams
ideas: Develop additional product lines (different generator types or sizes)
Offer financing or leasing for RV sales
Add complementary components to generators to save customer manufacturing steps

categories.name: Cost — COGS
ideas: Invest in manufacturing technology to reduce per-unit cost

categories.name: Cost — Fixed / SG&A
ideas: Reduce wages or renegotiate labor contracts

recommendation: Bob should launch a lower-quality, lower-priced generator before Company A enters the market
Scenario analysis shows launching the new generator yields $9.1M profit vs. only $1M profit if Bob does nothing and loses 45% of sales to the competitor
risks: Cost of developing the new generator was not examined — development capex could reduce actual profit
The competitor may still enter the market even if Bob launches a lower-quality product, triggering further price competition
Cannibalization of the high-margin existing generator (45% of volume) reduces blended margins permanently
next_steps: Quantify development cost for the new generator and update the profit comparison
Explore the revenue ideas surfaced in brainstorming: new customers, direct-to-consumer channel, adjacent markets
Investigate cost reduction opportunities (supplier negotiations, manufacturing efficiency) to restore margins
